hints: Think about what makes the d-block special, focus on the d orbitals and whether they are full, empty or partly filled in the element or its ions.
walkthrough:
Pin down the key test**
You are looking for a d-block metal that does not just have an incomplete d shell as an atom, but keeps it incomplete in at least one stable ion it forms. That is why zinc and scandium are excluded, their common ions have full or empty d shells.
Final answer: A transition element forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled (3)d subshell.

hints: Picture the five 3d orbitals in an isolated gaseous ion with no ligands around, there is nothing to split them so compare their energies.
walkthrough:
Visualise isolated orbitals**
With no ligands approaching, all five 3d orbitals experience the same environment. So they remain identical in energy. That equal energy idea is exactly what degenerate means.
Final answer: Degenerate means the orbitals are at the same energy.

hints: Start from copper atom $1s^22s^22p^63s^23p^63d^{10}4s^1$ and remember 4s electrons are removed before 3d when forming ions.
walkthrough:
Remove electrons in the right order**
Copper atom is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10} 4s^1$. To make $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, you lose the $4s^1$ electron first, then one $3d$ electron. That leaves $3d^9$ with the full inner shells unchanged, giving $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^9$.

hints: Recall the two classic copper(II) colour changes, adding excess ammonia to blue copper solution and adding concentrated HCl.
walkthrough:
Link ligand to colour memory**
The tetraammine copper(II) ion is famous as a deep dark royal blue solution, formed with excess ammonia. The tetrachlorocuprate(II) ion formed in concentrated HCl is yellow. Learn these as fixed colour pairs for copper.
Final answer: $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}\text{(aq)}$ deep / dark / royal blue and $\text{[CuCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}\text{(aq)}$ yellow.

hints: Think what happens to the equal energy d orbitals when ligands approach, do they stay degenerate or split into two sets?
Consider what a d electron can do if it absorbs exactly the right amount of energy from visible light.
Relate the colour you see to the colour that is removed by absorption, the observed colour is what is left over.
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
When ligands surround the metal ion, they repel d electrons unequally. Some d orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised in energy, others point between and stay lower. So the once degenerate set splits into two levels with a gap $\Delta E$.

Promote an electron across the gap**
A $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion is $3d^9$, so there is a vacancy in the upper set. An electron from the lower d set can absorb a photon with energy exactly equal to $\Delta E$ and jump up. This is a d-d transition.

See what is left over**
White light minus the absorbed colour leaves the complementary colour. Different ligands give different $\Delta E$, so different wavelengths are absorbed, which is why $\text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+}$ and $\text{[CuCl}_4\text{]}^{2-}$ have different colours.

Final answer: Ligands cause the d subshell to split into orbitals of different energy.
An electron is promoted / excited from a lower to a higher d orbital.
A specific wavelength / frequency of visible light is absorbed and the complementary / remaining colour is seen.

hints: Identify the process where $\text{Cl}^-$ ligands are swapped for $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ without change in oxidation state.
Balance ligands and charge by counting $\text{Cl}$, $\text{N}$, $\text{H}$ and $\text{O}$ on both sides, water is also a reactant here.
walkthrough:
Name the reaction type**
Copper stays as +2, no redox happens. You are simply swapping one set of ligands ($\text{Cl}^-$) for another set ($\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$). That is ligand exchange, also called substitution or displacement.

Balance the equation**
The product needs $4 \times \text{NH}_3$ and $2 \times \text{H}_2\text{O}$, so put those on the left. Four $\text{Cl}^-$ ions are released on the right. Check charge: $-2$ on left, $+2 -4 = -2$ on right. Atoms and charge both balance.

Final answer: Type: ligand exchange / substitution / replacement / displacement.
$\text{[CuCl}_4\text{]}^{2-} + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{[Cu(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^-$

hints: Picture an octahedral $\text{Cu}$ with four $\text{NH}_3$ in a plane and two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ that can be opposite each other or next to each other.
Use solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines to show 3D positions, one isomer has $180^{\circ}$ $\text{O-Cu-O}$ angle, the other has $90^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Draw the trans form**
Put $\text{Cu}$ in the centre. Place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite, one straight up and one straight down ($180^{\circ}$ apart). Then place the four $\text{NH}_3$ ligands in the plane around $\text{Cu}$, using wedges and dashes for front and back. This is trans-$\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{(NH}_3\text{)}_4\text{]}^{2+}$.

Draw the cis form**
Keep $\text{Cu}$ central but now put the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands next to each other at $90^{\circ}$, for example one up and one to the side in wedge. Fill the remaining four octahedral positions with $\text{NH}_3$. This different spatial arrangement is cis and cannot be superimposed on trans.

Final answer: Isomer 1 (trans): two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ opposite each other, e.g. axial positions, four $\text{NH}_3$ in equatorial plane.
Isomer 2 (cis): two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ adjacent at $90^{\circ}$, e.g. one axial one equatorial, with correct 3D wedge / dash bonds.

hints: Compare symmetry, in which isomer do the polar $\text{Cu-O}$ and $\text{Cu-N}$ bond dipoles cancel and in which do they leave a net dipole?
walkthrough:
Check symmetry for cancellation**
In trans, the two identical $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands pull equally in opposite directions, so their bond dipoles cancel and the molecule is non-polar. In cis, they pull at $90^{\circ}$, so there is a net dipole. Therefore cis is polar.
Final answer: cis isomer is polar because dipoles do not cancel.

hints: Look at structure P for atoms with lone pairs that can donate, focus on the two carboxylate oxygens and the central nitrogen.
walkthrough:
Spot the three donor atoms**
Each $\text{-COO}^-$ group has an oxygen with lone pairs ready to donate, that gives two donor oxygens. The central $\text{N-H}$ nitrogen also has a lone pair. Together they provide three lone pairs, so P binds at three sites and is tridentate.
Final answer: Two oxygen atoms and one nitrogen atom each donate a lone pair of electrons to the metal ion to form three dative covalent bonds.

hints: Add charges: $\text{Co}^{3+}$ plus two $2-$ ligands, what is the overall charge on the complex Q?
walkthrough:
Combine metal and ligands**
Two moles of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_5\text{NO}_4^{2-}$ give total $-4$. With one $\text{Co}^{3+}$, the net charge is $+3 + 2(-2) = -1$. Water ligands are all displaced, so Q is $\text{[Co(C}_4\text{H}_5\text{NO}_4\text{)}_2\text{]}^-$.

hints: Think of $K_{stab}$ as an equilibrium constant, what reaction does it describe, formation of the complex from what species?
walkthrough:
Define formation clearly**
$K_{stab}$ tells you how far the equilibrium lies for building the complex from the free hydrated metal ion plus free ligands, for example $\text{Ag}^+\text{(aq)} + 2\text{CN}^-\text{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \text{[Ag(CN)}_2\text{]}^-\text{(aq)}$. Larger $K_{stab}$ means more stable complex.
Final answer: Equilibrium constant for the formation of the complex ion in solution / water from its constituent metal ion and ligands.

hints: Scan Table 1.1 for the largest power of ten, larger $K_{stab}$ means the formation equilibrium lies furthest to the right.
walkthrough:
Pick the biggest K**
Compare $1.1 \times 10^{18}$, $1.2 \times 10^{7}$ and $2.9 \times 10^{13}$. The cyanide complex has by far the largest value, so its formation is most complete and it is the most stable.
Final answer: $\text{[Ag(CN)}_2\text{]}^-\text{(aq)}$ with largest $K_{stab}$ value of $1.1 \times 10^{18}$.

hints: Start with moles of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ used: $c \times V$ with $V$ in $\text{dm}^3$.
Use the equation ratio $2\text{MnO}_4^- : 5\text{SO}_3^{2-}$ to find moles of sulfite in the $10.0\text{ cm}^3$ aliquot, then scale up by $250/10$.
Convert total moles of $\text{SO}_3^{2-}$ to mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$ using $M_r = 126.1$ then express as percentage of $3.75\text{ g}$.
walkthrough:
Find moles of manganate(VII) titrated**
Use $n = cV$:
$$n(\text{MnO}_4^-) = 0.015 \times \frac{18.70}{1000} = 2.805 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
This is the amount that reacted with the $10.0\text{ cm}^3$ aliquot.

Apply stoichiometry then scale to the flask**
From the equation $2\text{MnO}_4^- \equiv 5\text{SO}_3^{2-}$:
$$n(\text{SO}_3^{2-})_{10.0} = 2.805 \times 10^{-4} \times \frac{5}{2} = 7.0125 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$$
The flask holds $250\text{ cm}^3$, which is $25$ times the aliquot:
$$n(\text{SO}_3^{2-})_{250} = 7.0125 \times 10^{-4} \times 25 = 1.753 \times 10^{-2} \text{ mol}$$

Convert to mass and percentage purity**
$M_r(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3) = 126.1$:
$$m = 1.753 \times 10^{-2} \times 126.1 = 2.21\text{ g}$$
$$\% = \frac{2.21}{3.75} \times 100 = 58.9\%$$
Keep at least 2 significant figures and include % sign.
